summary:
I've been building out BudgetTracker pretty heavily over the past couple of weeks — the app that tracks my spending, receipts, and subscriptions. The most interesting recent addition is a read-only MCP tool surface that lets Hermes, my local AI agent, query the app directly. It's 13 tools now: things like upcoming obligations, cash flow projection, burn rate against my budget, and a daily briefing endpoint. Hermes calls those over bearer-authenticated HTTP, gets back deterministic SQL-computed numbers, and phrases a notification or briefing section from them. The LLM never does the math; it just formats the result.

The income detection work that went in this week was the kind of problem that looks simple until you look at the data. I needed the projection tool to know when my next paycheck lands, but the recurring-detection pipeline had always been expense-only — income deposits were sitting in the database with nothing ever turning their cadence into a schedule. The fix was a new detection pass that scans income transactions grouped by merchant, fits a biweekly or monthly cadence using an interval median over the last 12 deposits, then proposes a schedule to confirm. Two bugs only appeared on a real-data smoke test: a gap-based day-of-month clustering method that collapsed 98 clean biweekly deposits into a false semimonthly pattern, and a history-gap issue where pay raises and a short gap made the full-history variance fail the consistency check. Both passed synthetic tests, caught on real data.

Also went through a security pass on BudgetTracker — path traversal on receipt uploads (a `..%2f` sequence was an authenticated arbitrary file read), JWT token-type separation so a refresh token can't be used as a Bearer access token, and upload content verification by magic bytes rather than declared MIME type. The interesting design question was LLM endpoint SSRF: the app lets users bring their own LLM API key, which means a user-supplied base URL. The guard I landed on is operator-vs-user, not private-vs-public IP — the server's own model (set by environment variable) is exempt, but any user-typed URL must be public HTTPS.

On the infrastructure side, I spun up a dedicated dev box — an old EliteDesk that was sitting unused — with Caddy handling wildcard `*.dev` routing, Docker, Tailscale, and five local dev environments running behind it: BudgetTracker on a local Postgres, the grocery list, the D&D app on a self-hosted Supabase stack, TheWordGroup on a local MSSQL container, and phillipsben.com. The self-hosted Supabase leg was the awkward part — the app uses Supabase Auth and Storage, so I couldn't just swap the connection string; I had to run the full Kong/GoTrue/storage stack alongside the app, with a second Caddy route for the API subdomain because the browser bundle has the URL baked in at build time and mixed-content blocks a plain HTTP reference from HTTPS.

highlights.oneLiner: Adding income pattern detection, MCP tool surface (13 tools), and a security hardening pass
Spinning up a dedicated dev box with Caddy wildcard routing and 5 local dev environments
Swapped brain to qwen3.6:35b, trimmed toolset 32K→20K tokens, scoped Telegram toolset for faster turns
Running TheWordGroup locally on dev01 behind Caddy against an isolated MSSQL container
